lead: A power series is an infinite polynomial, Σ cₙ(x−a)ⁿ, where a is a fixed centre and cₙ are fixed coefficients. Put in a value of x and you get a numerical series, which may converge or diverge. The surprise is that the x values that work always form one interval centred at a, and its half-width is the radius of convergence R. Most scientific calculators and numerical libraries compute sin x, eˣ and log x from short polynomial approximations built from these series.
prereq: You need: sequences (3.1), series (3.2), the ratio and root tests (3.3), the Leibnitz test (3.4) and absolute convergence (3.5).

sections.h3: Definition and the shape of the convergence set

blocks.text: Fix a real number a, called the centre, and a sequence of real numbers c₀, c₁, c₂, … called the coefficients. The expression Σ cₙ(x−a)ⁿ is a power series in (x−a). The variable is x; a and all the cₙ stay fixed.

blocks.where: a is the centre; cₙ is the coefficient of (x−a)ⁿ; x is the variable. Some syllabi call the case a = 0 a power series in x.

blocks.text: For example Σ xⁿ/n! has a = 0 and cₙ = 1/n!. Putting x = 2 turns it into the numerical series Σ 2ⁿ/n!, which is judged by the rules of 3.2.

The set of x where it converges has a rigid shape. Suppose the series converges at some point b ≠ a. Then cₙ(b−a)ⁿ → 0, so these terms are bounded: there is M with |cₙ(b−a)ⁿ| ≤ M for every n. Take any x with |x−a| < |b−a| and write r = |x−a|/|b−a|, so 0 ≤ r < 1. Then |cₙ(x−a)ⁿ| ≤ M rⁿ, and Σ M rⁿ is a convergent geometric series. Comparison gives absolute convergence at x.

So convergence at one point drags in every point closer to a, and the convergence set is centred at a: either the single point a, or an interval (a−R, a+R) with either end possibly included, or the whole real line. One number, the radius of convergence R, measures it. R is a distance, so R ≥ 0, and R = ∞ is allowed.
Hold x fixed and write uₙ = cₙ(x−a)ⁿ for the nth term. The ratio test of 3.3 compares consecutive terms.

blocks.where: L = lim_{n→∞} |cₙ₊₁/cₙ|, assumed to exist; x ≠ a so that division is allowed.

blocks.text: The ratio test gives absolute convergence when L|x−a| < 1 and divergence when L|x−a| > 1. Read the first condition as |x−a| < 1/L. That half-width is the radius.

blocks.where: R is the radius of convergence; cₙ, cₙ₊₁ are consecutive coefficients. If the limit is 0 then R = 0; if the limit is ∞ then R = ∞.

blocks.text: When this limit fails, or some cₙ are zero, the root test of 3.3 still works.

blocks.where: limsup is the largest limit point of the sequence |cₙ|^(1/n); take R = ∞ when it is 0 and R = 0 when it is ∞.

items: Σ n! xⁿ: cₙ = n!, so |cₙ/cₙ₊₁| = 1/(n+1) → 0 and R = 0. Only x = 0 works.
Σ xⁿ/n!: |cₙ/cₙ₊₁| = n+1 → ∞, so R = ∞ and every x works.
Mind the direction: R = lim |cₙ/cₙ₊₁|, not lim |cₙ₊₁/cₙ|. The flipped limit equals 1/R.

sections.h3: Endpoints and the interval of convergence

blocks.text: For |x−a| < R the series converges absolutely. For |x−a| > R it diverges, and the terms do not even tend to 0. At |x−a| = R the ratio test returns exactly 1, its inconclusive case, so the two endpoints need separate work.

At x = a + R the series becomes the numerical series Σ cₙRⁿ; at x = a − R it becomes Σ cₙ(−R)ⁿ. Test each one on its own, using comparison, the integral test or the Leibnitz test (3.4) and absolute convergence (3.5). Both may converge, both may diverge, or one may do each.
The full answer is the interval of convergence: (a−R, a+R), [a−R, a+R), (a−R, a+R] or [a−R, a+R], depending on the two endpoint verdicts.

Inside R the series defines a function f(x) = Σ cₙ(x−a)ⁿ, and f can be differentiated and integrated term by term; the new series keeps the same R, though its endpoints may move. Taylor's theorem in Unit 1 builds such series for known functions; this chapter runs the other way, from coefficients to the x values that work.

One use: Σ xⁿ/n at the endpoint x = −1 gives −ln 2 ≈ −0.6931, so ln 2 = 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − ⋯. Calculators evaluate sin, cos and eˣ the same way, with x kept inside a small interval where a few terms are enough.

figure.caption: The coefficients give R = 1 for the series in the worked example; that fixes the open interval |x| < 1 at once, while x = −1 and x = 1 must be tested separately and are then included or dropped one by one.

spec.title: Radius and interval for Σ xⁿ/n
spec.aria: A flow that finds R = 1 from the coefficients of the series Σ xⁿ/n, marks the open interval |x| < 1, and then tests the two endpoints before writing the interval as [−1, 1).

examples.question: Find the radius of convergence and the interval of convergence of Σ_{n=1}^{∞} xⁿ/n. At x = −1, state the sum of the resulting series.
steps: Identify the centre and coefficients: a = 0, cₙ = 1/n, and the nth term is uₙ = xⁿ/n.
Let n → ∞: n/(n+1) → 1, so the limit is |x|. The ratio test gives absolute convergence for |x| < 1 and divergence for |x| > 1. Hence R = 1.
Check with the coefficient formula: R = lim |cₙ/cₙ₊₁| = lim (1/n) ÷ (1/(n+1)) = lim (n+1)/n = 1. Same answer.
Endpoint x = 1: the series becomes Σ 1/n, the harmonic series, which diverges (integral test or comparison).
Endpoint x = −1: the series becomes Σ (−1)ⁿ/n. The sizes bₙ = 1/n decrease to 0, so the Leibnitz test gives convergence. Since Σ 1/n diverges, this convergence is conditional.
Assemble: include −1, exclude 1. The interval of convergence is [−1, 1).
examples.answer: R = 1, the interval of convergence is [−1, 1), and at x = −1 the series sums to −ln 2 ≈ −0.6931.
examples.check:
import math
n = 10**6
print(round((n + 1) / n, 4))
s = sum((-1)**k / k for k in range(1, 200001))
print(round(s, 4))

traps: Stopping at R = 1 and writing (−1, 1). The endpoints x = −1 and x = 1 are separate numerical series and can answer differently; here −1 is in and 1 is out.
Flipping the coefficient ratio. R = lim |cₙ/cₙ₊₁|; writing lim |cₙ₊₁/cₙ| gives 1/R and a wrong interval.
Forgetting the shift. Σ (x−2)ⁿ/3ⁿ has R = 3 and centre 2, so the open interval is (−1, 5), not (−3, 3).
Assuming both endpoints behave alike, or that endpoint convergence is absolute. At x = −1 the series Σ (−1)ⁿ/n converges only conditionally, because Σ 1/n diverges.
Applying the ratio test to cₙ alone, without the factor |x−a|, and then declaring the whole series convergent instead of finding R.

quiz.q: Define a power series with centre a, naming the coefficients and the variable.
quiz.a: Σ_{n=0}^{∞} cₙ(x−a)ⁿ, where a is the fixed centre, c₀, c₁, c₂, … are fixed real coefficients, and x is the variable.

quiz.q: State the formula for R when lim |cₙ/cₙ₊₁| exists, including the extreme cases.
quiz.a: R = lim_{n→∞} |cₙ/cₙ₊₁|. If the limit is 0 then R = 0; if the limit is ∞ then R = ∞.

quiz.q: Why must the set of convergence be an interval centred at a, and not two separate pieces?
quiz.a: Convergence at a point b makes cₙ(b−a)ⁿ bounded, and then comparison with the geometric series Σ M rⁿ, r = |x−a|/|b−a| < 1, gives absolute convergence at every x closer to a than b. So every point pulls in all points nearer the centre.

quiz.q: Find R and the interval of convergence of Σ (x−3)ⁿ/2ⁿ.
quiz.a: Here cₙ = 1/2ⁿ, so |cₙ/cₙ₊₁| = 2 and R = 2 with centre 3. Endpoints: x = 1 and x = 5 give Σ (±1)ⁿ, whose terms do not tend to 0, so both diverge. Interval of convergence: (1, 5).

quiz.q: Find R and the interval of convergence of Σ n xⁿ.
quiz.a: cₙ = n, so |cₙ/cₙ₊₁| = n/(n+1) → 1 and R = 1 with centre 0. At x = 1 the term is n, at x = −1 the term is (−1)ⁿ n; neither tends to 0, so both endpoints diverge. Interval: (−1, 1).

quiz.q: Σ xⁿ/n and Σ xⁿ/n² have the same R. Do they have the same interval of convergence?
quiz.a: Both have R = 1. At x = 1 they give Σ 1/n (divergent) and Σ 1/n² (convergent). At x = −1 both converge, the first conditionally and the second absolutely. Intervals: [−1, 1) and [−1, 1]. Same radius, different interval, so R never settles the endpoints.

quiz.q: Σ cₙxⁿ converges at x = 3. What follows at x = −2, and why?
quiz.a: Convergence at x = 3 forces R ≥ 3, since points beyond R cannot converge. Now |−2| = 2 < 3 ≤ R, so x = −2 lies strictly inside the interval and the series converges absolutely there.

beyond: Not for the exam. Put a complex z in place of x and the same R describes a disc |z−a| < R, whose boundary is far wilder than two points. Functions that are locally sums of power series are called analytic, and they are the central objects of complex analysis. In combinatorics, generating functions pack a whole sequence into the coefficients of a power series and answer counting problems by algebra on the series. In signal processing, the z-transform is a Laurent series whose region of convergence decides whether the transform exists. Numerical libraries compute sin and exp with short polynomial approximations cut from power series. Search next: radius of convergence, analytic function, z-transform region of convergence.
